PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
CON
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
This is the November 2026 California ballot measure, Proposition 43, a legislative constitutional amendment that would require two-thirds voter approval for voter-initiated local special taxes starting in 2027.

I'm looking at who backs and opposes this measure: the California Taxpayers Association and business groups on one side, firefighters, teachers, and nurses' unions on the other. The page says it would raise the vote needed for voter-proposed local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds starting January 1, 2027.

I'm checking whether this measure is really the 2026 legislative amendment I half-remember, since the two-thirds requirement for local special taxes doesn't quite match ACA 13's threshold-protection purpose. I'll look into whether this is a separate deal-based measure before weighing which side is likely to prevail.

I'm working out what the yes/no answer should map to, since "which side" doesn't fit a single yes or no. The likeliest reading is that "yes" means the Yes side, the supporters of Prop 43, wins, which amounts to the proposition passing, and "no" means the No side wins.

I'm settling how to read the yes/no answer: "yes" means Prop 43 passes, which is the same as the Yes side winning, and "no" means it fails. Since the user wants only one of those two words, I'll give that and nothing more.

Next I'm searching for polls, endorsements, and campaign spending on Prop 43 to see how the measure is trending.

I'm comparing this to past California measures: Prop 5 and Prop 33 failed in 2024, while Prop 36 passed, and taxpayer-backed measures like Props 13, 218, and 26 have historically won.

Checking the remaining bit on Prop 32 from 2024: the result was close, with the No side winning narrowly, and I'll look up the exact vote split and the campaign finance and endorsement details for Prop 43 next.

Now I'm also weighing whether the Legislature placed this amendment as part of a deal to head off a taxpayer initiative, and I'll look into that alongside the other propositions on the November ballot.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
PROPOSAL
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.
Visit sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/cal-access-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/cal-access-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals) for a list of committees primarily formed to support or oppose this measure.
Visit fppc.ca.gov/transparency/top-contributors.html (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/transparency/top-contributors.html) to access the committee's top 10 contributors.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES
Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes-using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.
These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.
Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.
PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES
California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.
Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.
Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.
PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS
Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety-only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.
If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.
PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE
Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.
Vote YES on Prop. 43:
• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Robert Rivinius , President
Family Business Association of California
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
We all want relief from California’s high cost of living. But Proposition 43 doesn’t cut your taxes a penny. It attacks something far more valuable: the power of your vote.
PROP. 43 WEAKENS YOUR VOTE.
Today, when local voters decide how to fund their communities, the majority rules. Prop. 43 throws that out, letting just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Under Prop. 43, a NO vote counts twice as much as a YES. That isn’t fair, and it isn’t democracy.
PROP. 43 DEEPENS THE HOUSING CRISIS.
Across California, communities vote to build affordable homes for working families, seniors, and veterans. They are helping renters stay housed and move people off the streets. Prop. 43 hands a small minority the power to block those solutions, even when a clear majority of your neighbors support them.
PROP. 43 TIES YOUR COMMUNITY’S HANDS.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund the critical local services your community counts on: staffing fire stations and 911 response, preparing neighborhoods for wildfire, repairing crumbling roads, keeping schools, parks, and libraries open, and protecting local hospitals and clinics as Washington cuts healthcare funding. When funding is blocked, help arrives slower, classrooms grow more crowded, and communities are left less safe.
KEEP THE POWER WHERE IT BELONGS-WITH YOU AND YOUR NEIGHBORS.
That’s why teachers, nurses, firefighters, and housing advocates all oppose Prop. 43.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Nick Lapis , Director of Advocacy
Californians Against Waste
Bill Barnes , Director of Campaigns & Community
Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California
Steve Frisch , President
Sierra Business Council
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 43
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES.
Prop. 43 makes it harder for you to fund critical services like police and fire departments, fix and repair local roads, staff our local schools or backfill federal healthcare cuts. Prop. 43 undermines the voice of voters and the majority vote by letting just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions-and it makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FUND FIRE AND POLICE SERVICES.
Local police and firefighters can’t rely on Sacramento or Washington politicians. These services are funded at the local level. Prop. 43 wants to make it harder for local voters to direct new funding to services like police and fire. Without adequate funding, 911 response times are slower, fire stations sit understaffed, and families wait longer for help when every second counts. When a house fire breaks out-or a wildfire threatens our neighborhoods-that local funding is what protects us. Prop. 43 would let a small minority of voters block it. Even if 66% of voters say yes, Prop. 43 would prevent us from funding desperately needed local services.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FIX ROADS, FUND SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.
Across California, local voters have come together to repair crumbling roads and improve transportation, to fund their neighborhood schools, and to protect local hospitals and healthcare-especially as Washington cuts federal health funding. These are decisions communities make for themselves, by majority vote. Instead, Prop. 43 hands a small group of voters the power to veto those solutions, even when the majority supports them.
PROP. 43 EMPOWERS 33.4% OF VOTERS OVER THE WILL OF THE MAJORITY.
In America, we believe in one person, one vote-and the majority wins. Prop. 43 throws that out. It empowers just over one-third of voters to block what nearly 67% want. It puts the out-voted minority in charge-even if they are extremists. It makes their NO vote count twice as much as a YES vote.
CORPORATE DONORS BENEFIT. NOT TAXPAYERS.
Under Prop. 43, corporate donors who spend big in elections will benefit most. Right now, voters can hold these corporations and developers accountable at the ballot box, and make them pay their fair share for local needs. Prop. 43 is designed to take that power away-to protect the powerful few, at everyone else’s expense.
That’s why these organizations are asking you to vote NO on Prop. 43:
• California Professional Firefighters • Californians Against Waste • California Federation of Teachers • California School Employees Association • Communities for a Better Environment • AAPI Force • Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California • Nurses Alliance of SEIU California • Sierra Business Council
Vote NO to protect your vote and majority rule. Keep the power where it belongs-with you and your neighbors.
VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 43.
www.NoProp43CA.com
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Harkins , Executive Director
Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
Adam Weinberger , President
California School Employees Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43 TO RESTORE TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Californians already pay high taxes. But instead of prioritizing funding for critical services like police and fire, local politicians waste your money on their pet projects- then demand tax increases, claiming the need to fund the most important priorities.
The state Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, but recent court decisions created a loophole that allowed special taxes to pass with fewer votes. Now Californians are paying billions in taxes they should not have had to pay.
Prop. 43 RESTORES the longstanding two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes, protecting homeowners, renters, and small businesses from costly new sales and parcel taxes, taxes on electricity and gas, and real estate taxes.
Prop. 43 GUARANTEES taxpayers the right to vote on new or higher local taxes and requires governments to spend taxpayer dollars for the specific purposes voters approved-preventing bait-and-switch schemes that make our sky-high cost of living even worse.
Over the last decade, local governments have imposed 2,000 new or higher taxes. Prop. 43 CLOSES LOOPHOLES used to pass some of the most damaging tax increases, restores the protections voters originally approved under Proposition 13, and makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes without broad voter support.
The Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot sends a clear message: activist courts exceeded voters’ intent by creating loopholes that weakened Proposition 13’s protections.
Restore your right to vote on ALL local taxes.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Greg Van Dyke , Chairman
California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and
Safety

# Proposition 43
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
PROPOSAL
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES
Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes-using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.
These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.
Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.
PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES
California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.
Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.
Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.
PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS
Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety-only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.
If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.
PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE
Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.
Vote YES on Prop. 43:
• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.

VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS

Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.

content.thinking:
This is the November 2026 California ballot measure, Proposition 43, a legislative constitutional amendment that would require two-thirds voter approval for voter-initiated local special taxes starting in 2027.

I'm looking at who backs and opposes this measure: the California Taxpayers Association and business groups on one side, firefighters, teachers, and nurses' unions on the other. The page says it would raise the vote needed for voter-proposed local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds starting January 1, 2027.

I'm checking whether this measure is really the 2026 legislative amendment I half-remember, since the two-thirds requirement for local special taxes doesn't quite match ACA 13's threshold-protection purpose. I'll look into whether this is a separate deal-based measure before weighing which side is likely to prevail.

I'm working out what the yes/no answer should map to, since "which side" doesn't fit a single yes or no. The likeliest reading is that "yes" means the Yes side, the supporters of Prop 43, wins, which amounts to the proposition passing, and "no" means the No side wins.

I'm settling how to read the yes/no answer: "yes" means Prop 43 passes, which is the same as the Yes side winning, and "no" means it fails. Since the user wants only one of those two words, I'll give that and nothing more.

Next I'm searching for polls, endorsements, and campaign spending on Prop 43 to see how the measure is trending.

I'm comparing this to past California measures: Prop 5 and Prop 33 failed in 2024, while Prop 36 passed, and taxpayer-backed measures like Props 13, 218, and 26 have historically won.

Checking the remaining bit on Prop 32 from 2024: the result was close, with the No side winning narrowly, and I'll look up the exact vote split and the campaign finance and endorsement details for Prop 43 next.

Now I'm also weighing whether the Legislature placed this amendment as part of a deal to head off a taxpayer initiative, and I'll look into that alongside the other propositions on the November ballot.

# Proposition 43
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors).
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time.
Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

# 2026 California Proposition 43
**Proposition 43** is a proposed legislative constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.
Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under Proposition 13 for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local initiative power.^[1]^ Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the California Constitution.^[2]^
Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the California Supreme Court,^[3]^ which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13.
These appellate court rulings held that citizen-led special tax proposals under the local initiative power were no longer subject to the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13.

PROP
43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Local Governments in California. California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.
Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes. The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.
PROPOSAL
Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters. Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are proposed by voters to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future. Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 43
VOTE YES ON PROP. 43: THE LOCAL TAXPAYER PROTECTION ACT
California families are struggling with the highest income, sales, and gas taxes in the nation. Yet politicians and special interests keep pushing higher taxes that make our cost of living even more expensive.
We can’t afford to pay ANY MORE in new or higher taxes. PROP. 43 RESTORES PROPOSITION 13 TAXPAYER PROTECTIONS
Proposition 13 was designed to make it harder to raise taxes, but court decisions created loopholes that allow special interests to impose massive new tax increases by circumventing the taxpayer protections voters approved. Californians are paying billions in new or higher taxes they would not have to pay if it weren’t for these loopholes. Prop. 43 closes these loopholes and restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO RAISE YOUR TAXES
Local governments have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade, including higher sales, property and utility taxes-using the loopholes courts created in Prop. 13 to impose some of the most costly and damaging tax increases Californians face today.
These new and higher taxes make everything we buy or use more expensive, from food and gas to utilities and housing.
Prop. 43 guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes and restores the two-thirds vote for special local taxes.
PROP. 43 PROTECTS HOMEOWNERS FROM COSTLY NEW REAL ESTATE TAXES
California already has some of the highest housing costs in America, yet special interests are using court-created loopholes to add new taxes on the sale of homes, apartments and other real estate.
Some cities now charge real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%. For California’s median-priced home of $900,000, that would cost a homeowner $54,000 simply for selling their house. Those costs steal homeowners’ equity, raise apartment rents, and make building new housing more expensive.
Prop. 43 makes it much harder for special interests to impose these costly taxes on homeowners, renters, and small businesses.
PROP. 43 STOPS THE BAIT-AND-SWITCH TAX TRICKS
Politicians and special interests promise new taxes will fund schools, roads, and public safety-only to divert the money elsewhere and frustrate the will of voters. Prop. 43 requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved and restores the broad voter support required before politicians and special interests impose earmarked tax measures.
If taxpayers are asked to pay more, they deserve the right to vote and the confidence their money will be spent as promised.
PROP. 43 PUTS VOTERS BACK IN CHARGE
Every election, politicians say they need just one more tax increase. Prop. 43 simply ensures TAXPAYERS are fully protected by the right to vote on taxes.
Vote YES on Prop. 43:
• Affirms the voters’ right to vote on all new or higher local taxes. • Restores the two-thirds vote requirement for local special taxes. • Protects Proposition 13 and closes court-created loopholes. • Makes it harder for special interests to raise taxes. • Protects homeowners, renters, and small businesses from new real estate taxes. • Strengthens accountability for how taxpayer dollars are spent.

PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES.

Prop. 43 undermines the voice of voters and the majority vote by letting just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions-and it makes it easier for corporate special interests to avoid paying their fair share.
PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FUND FIRE AND POLICE SERVICES.

Prop. 43 wants to make it harder for local voters to direct new funding to services like police and fire. PROP. 43 MAKES IT HARDER TO FIX ROADS, FUND SCHOOLS, AND PROTECT HEALTHCARE.

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).

What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

I'm weighing Prop 43 now: it's ACA 22, a legislative referral that passed the Assembly 68-2 and was nearly unanimous overall, and it came out of a deal with HJTA to pull their Taxpayer Protection initiative off the ballot. The supporters I'm noting are CalTax, the Family Business Association, the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, HJTA, and the California Small Business Association.

I'm listing the opposition now: firefighters, Californians Against Waste, the teachers and school employees unions, several environmental and housing groups, and others. I also need to find out whether the SF Chronicle endorsed Yes or No, since the headline's wording could go either way. Berkeley's council has an urgency item opposing it, and a LAist update dated November 2, 2026 suggests the current date may be near or past the election.

I'm going to look for whether the election has already happened and any results are out, since I'm not sure what today's date is. I'll also search for polling on Prop 43 from groups like PPIC and Berkeley IGS.

# Proposition 43
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them.
...
### Proposal
***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved.
These are called special taxes.
However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote.
Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

California's Proposition 43 is asking voters to require a two-thirds vote for local special taxes that residents place on the ballot by petition.
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local special tax that residents place on the ballot by petition, the same threshold that already applies when a city council, county board or special district proposes one.
A special tax is one whose money is dedicated to a specific purpose, such as fire protection, parks, housing or schools.
Since a series of court rulings that began in 2017, voter-proposed special taxes have needed only a simple majority.
Prop 43 would end that for measures approved from January 1, 2027, and it leaves every tax already on the books in place.

Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027.
As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters.

This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax.
The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity.^1^Under California’s Constitution, *all taxes* levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop.
43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to *any* taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.

Prop 43: Special Tax Measure limits
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
Proposition 43 would make it harder to create or raise certain local taxes. It would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens from a simple majority to two-thirds. The measure grew out of a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.
What’s at stake
A two-thirds vote is already required for special taxes proposed by local governments, but not for those proposed by individual citizens. Prop. 43 would close that gap and apply the higher bar to citizen-led initiatives as well. That could affect how communities pay for local services through voter-approved taxes.
Official title on the ballot: Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) :
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027.
What your vote means
A “yes” vote means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
A “no” vote means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
Understanding Prop. 43
Special taxes are ones levied for a specific purpose, such as affordable housing or public transportation, while general taxes go into a city’s general fund and can be used for any city program or service. General taxes only require a simple majority to pass, regardless of who places them on the ballot.
But special taxes placed on the ballot by a local government must meet the two-thirds approval threshold. For a long time, it was assumed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) that special taxes from citizen-led initiatives had to meet this higher mark. That changed in 2017 (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/), and now these initiatives only need to win over 50% of the vote.
Since then, municipalities have passed over two dozen of these initiatives with support below the two-thirds mark, according to previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/). In Los Angeles, the most high-profile recent example is Measure ULA (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure), also known as the “mansion tax,” (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote) which passed in 2022 with 57.77% of the vote (https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300).
Watch the ballot cram session analysis
What supporters say
Anti-tax advocates have pushed for similar policies for years. They argue that special interest groups have taken advantage of the simple-majority threshold to pass special taxes in low-turnout elections.
Notable supporters: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Reform California and the Southern California News Group editorial board
What opponents say
Opponents argue the measure would limit communities’ ability to raise needed money for local services. They also say it would make it easier for wealthy interests to block tax measures that most voters support.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000 and The Sacramento Bee editorial board
Fiscal impact
Because Prop. 43 would make it more difficult to pass certain taxes, local governments’ tax revenues “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be,” according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=43&year=2026), which says the precise impact would “depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.”

There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

2026 elections: Track results for all 14 California propositions
This November, California voters will make choices on a variety of issues — from housing to elections, healthcare and taxes.
Ashley Zavala (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Political Director (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Nijzel Dotson
Digital Producer
There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

2026 elections: Track results for all 14 California propositions
This November, California voters will make choices on a variety of issues — from housing to elections, healthcare and taxes.
Ashley Zavala (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Political Director (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Nijzel Dotson
Digital Producer
There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

I'm looking at the latest polling for Prop 43: the PPIC October survey has it at 42% yes and 55% no, down from 43% and 51% in September. The UC Berkeley IGS poll shows 36% yes and 46% no, also a slight slide from September's 31% and 40%. I'm also starting on the campaign finance figures, with the yes side around $15.3M.

I'm checking whether the KCRA results page has actual numbers yet, since the azcentral page came back empty. I still need to pin down today's date, because if the vote has already happened, the results would settle which side wins.

Political Director (https://www.kcra.com/news-team/21271fb1-6e06-4bcf-8b56-97b158a0e14b)
Nijzel Dotson
Digital Producer
There are 14 propositions on the General Election ballot (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/).
Five of the measures are related to taxes, three are related to elections and campaigns, three ask voters to borrow money for specific issues, and three make changes to state laws around spending, saving and environmentally related construction rules.
Advertisement
See live Election Day updates here (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-day-live-updates-nov-3/74317260)
Track full election results here (http://www.kcra.com/article/california-election-night-results-2026/74184627)
You can track the results below after polls close at 8 p.m.
PROPOSITION 1
If passed, Proposition 1, also known as the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, would approve $11.25 billion for low-income families, farmworkers, students, foster youth and veterans.
See Prop. 1 results:
PROPOSITION 2
Proposition 2 would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.
California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety and other critical services.
See Prop. 2 results:
PROPOSITION 3
California voters will decide whether to make a temporary higher state income tax on California's wealthiest taxpayers permanent. It's on this year's ballot as Proposition 3 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/index.htm).
Voters first approved the temporary tax in 2012 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx). It was renewed in 2016 (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). It's currently set to expire in 2031.
See Prop. 3 results:
PROPOSITION 4
Proposition 4 would allow cities and counties to set up public campaign financing. For those that do, politicians in that area can use the money for their campaigns as long as they meet certain thresholds.
See Prop. 4 results:
PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 would limit recall ballots to just one yes-or-no question: Should an elected official be recalled from office?
Currently, recall ballots also have a second section where voters are asked to choose a successor if the recall passes. Prop 5 would eliminate that second section. If the recall passes, a new leader is chosen later in a separate process.
See Prop. 5 results:
PROPOSITION 37
Proposition 37 proposes a $25 billion loan program to help California residents overcome the challenge of affording down payments on new homes.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37.pdf), authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg, would allow the state government to issue bonds to help residents borrow up to 17% of their down payment, requiring them to contribute at least 3% themselves, while their primary mortgage would cover the remaining 80%.
See Prop. 37 results:
PROPOSITION 38
Prop 38 would direct the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, which includes research on diseases such as cancer, Parkinson's, ALS and MS.
See Prop. 38 results:
PROPOSITION 39
Proposition 39 requires government-issued ID at the polls or the last four digits of the ID number for mail-in ballots. Elections officials would also be required to annually report the percentage of voters with verified citizenship.
See Prop. 39 results:
PROPOSITION 40
Proposition 40 asks voters to approve a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of California residents with a net worth of a billion dollars with the goal of raising $100 billion to fund mostly healthcare programs.
See Prop. 40 results:
PROPOSITION 41
Proposition 41 is in response to the proposed billionaire tax, requiring strict oversight of how new taxes are used and prohibiting any new taxes that are exempted from the state’s spending limit required under the state constitution, meaning it would cancel out the billionaire tax. The measure with the most votes becomes law.
See Prop. 41 results:
PROPOSITION 42
Proposition 42 would ban new state taxes on personal property and assets, including retirement accounts, personal savings, and investments.
If the billionaire tax through Prop 40 and either Proposition 41 or 42 pass, the measure with the most votes will become law.
See Prop. 42 results:
PROPOSITION 43
Proposition 43 would make it more difficult to pass new special taxes in cities and counties. Currently, local governments such as city councils or county supervisors can propose special taxes, which require approval by a two-thirds vote from residents. However, special taxes proposed by citizens or special interest groups only need a simple majority to pass.
See Prop. 43 results:
PROPOSITION 44
Proposition 44 aims at changing how community health clinics spend taxpayer dollars. Supporters say it will increase accountability, but opponents warn it could threaten services patients rely on.
See Prop. 44 results:
PROPOSITION 45
Proposition 45 would change parts of California's Environmental Quality Act to speed up environmental review of housing, transportation and other infrastructure projects. It would also limit the ability of lawsuits to stop or slow a project.
See Prop. 45 results:

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Election Day is here.
California voters are set to choose a new governor, vote on all other statewide offices and decide 14 propositions.
Advertisement
For this cycle, voters will also elect their U.S. representative using maps that were redrawn to favor Democrats. Californians adopted Proposition 50, which created maps using redrawn districts targeting five Republicans that in turn affected the boundaries of neighboring districts. The races could help decide the balance of power in Congress.
(See live coverage of Election Day starting at 4 a.m. PT in the video above.)
We'll keep updating this story with the latest information as Election Day unfolds.
What time do polls open and close on Election Day?
All California vote centers open Tuesday at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. for those who wish to vote in person or return their ballot there. Voters can also return their vote-by-mail ballot at secure dropbox locations.
California officials recommended that people who planned to mail their ballot get that done at least a week in advance. Mail must be postmarked on or before Nov. 3 to count.
Where can I find my polling place?
You can find a vote center on the back of your county voter information guide or by clicking here (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place).
The state is also offering a service where people can text "vote" to 468-683 (GOVOTE) to find their polling place.
‘It was so convenient’: Sacramento County's 92 vote centers are open for the Midterm Election (https://www.kcra.com/article/sacramento-county-vote-centers-open-for-election/74312369)
Get the Facts: Can federal agents be at polling places? What voters should know (https://www.kcra.com/article/get-the-facts-can-federal-agents-be-at-polling-places-what-voters-should-know/74277521)
What to know about the Election Day forecast
A cold front passing through will bring some periods of showers and Sierra snow across Northern California. Scattered showers should reach Sacramento and the surrounding area by late morning. Rain will start in the Foothills before noon. In the Sierra, expect rain and snow showers from midday into the early evening. See the full forecast here (https://www.kcra.com/article/northern-california-election-day-rain-snow-november-3/74313505).
Missed your voter registration date? California offers same-day registration
In California, the deadline to register to vote before an election is 15 days. However, if you miss the deadline, you can cast a ballot provisionally. California law states any voter whose qualifications cannot be immediately verified can cast a ballot provisionally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot.https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot). This process involves comparing the signature of the provisional ballot with the signature on the voter's affidavit of registration to ensure the person is properly registered to vote.
California also allows for same-day registration until 8 p.m. on Election Day. You can sign up for conditional voter registration at your county elections office, or any vote center or polling place in your county.
Track your vote in California
The Secretary of State's Office offers a way for voters to track their ballot online (https://wheresmyballot.sos.ca.gov/). The service allows people to receive updates when their ballot is mailed, received, counted or if an issue comes up. Voters will have the option of email, text or phone call updates.
How to track your ballot in California for the Nov. 3 midterm election (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-2026-general-election-ballot-tracker/74286952)

3. Jon Coupal: Proposition 43 is essential for taxpayer protection
https://www.ocregister.com/2026/10/23/jon-coupal-proposition-43-is-essential-for-taxpayer-protection/
# Jon Coupal: Proposition 43 is essential for taxpayer protection
...
Proposition 43 is a taxpayer protection measure that makes it harder to raise local special taxes, such as sales taxes, that are earmarked for a specific purpose.
But Prop.
43 is nothing new.
It merely restores what California voters have approved three times in the past but what was taken away by questionable court rulings.
For years, California’s Constitution was understood to require two-thirds voter approval for local special taxes.
That understanding began to change after the California Supreme Court’s 2017 decision in California Cannabis Coalition v.
City of Upland.
Although Upland concerned the timing of an initiative election, the court distinguished between taxes imposed by local government and those proposed by voters through the initiative process.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Election Day is here.
California voters are set to choose a new governor, vote on all other statewide offices and decide 14 propositions.
Advertisement
For this cycle, voters will also elect their U.S. representative using maps that were redrawn to favor Democrats. Californians adopted Proposition 50, which created maps using redrawn districts targeting five Republicans that in turn affected the boundaries of neighboring districts. The races could help decide the balance of power in Congress.
(See live coverage of Election Day starting at 4 a.m. PT in the video above.)
We'll keep updating this story with the latest information as Election Day unfolds.
What time do polls open and close on Election Day?
All California vote centers open Tuesday at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. for those who wish to vote in person or return their ballot there. Voters can also return their vote-by-mail ballot at secure dropbox locations.
California officials recommended that people who planned to mail their ballot get that done at least a week in advance. Mail must be postmarked on or before Nov. 3 to count.
Where can I find my polling place?
You can find a vote center on the back of your county voter information guide or by clicking here (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place).
The state is also offering a service where people can text "vote" to 468-683 (GOVOTE) to find their polling place.
‘It was so convenient’: Sacramento County's 92 vote centers are open for the Midterm Election (https://www.kcra.com/article/sacramento-county-vote-centers-open-for-election/74312369)
