What to know about the Election Day forecast
A cold front passing through will bring some periods of showers and Sierra snow across Northern California. Scattered showers should reach Sacramento and the surrounding area by late morning. Rain will start in the Foothills before noon. In the Sierra, expect rain and snow showers from midday into the early evening. See the full forecast here (https://www.kcra.com/article/northern-california-election-day-rain-snow-november-3/74313505).
Missed your voter registration date? California offers same-day registration
In California, the deadline to register to vote before an election is 15 days. However, if you miss the deadline, you can cast a ballot provisionally. California law states any voter whose qualifications cannot be immediately verified can cast a ballot provisionally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot.https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot). This process involves comparing the signature of the provisional ballot with the signature on the voter's affidavit of registration to ensure the person is properly registered to vote.
California also allows for same-day registration until 8 p.m. on Election Day. You can sign up for conditional voter registration at your county elections office, or any vote center or polling place in your county.
Track your vote in California
The Secretary of State's Office offers a way for voters to track their ballot online (https://wheresmyballot.sos.ca.gov/). The service allows people to receive updates when their ballot is mailed, received, counted or if an issue comes up. Voters will have the option of email, text or phone call updates.

# Jon Coupal: Proposition 43 is essential for taxpayer protection
...
Proposition 43 is a taxpayer protection measure that makes it harder to raise local special taxes, such as sales taxes, that are earmarked for a specific purpose.
But Prop.
43 is nothing new.
It merely restores what California voters have approved three times in the past but what was taken away by questionable court rulings.
For years, California’s Constitution was understood to require two-thirds voter approval for local special taxes.
That understanding began to change after the California Supreme Court’s 2017 decision in California Cannabis Coalition v.
City of Upland.
Although Upland concerned the timing of an initiative election, the court distinguished between taxes imposed by local government and those proposed by voters through the initiative process.
Subsequent decisions applied that reasoning to the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes.
The result is a loophole at the center of Proposition 13.
While a city council or county board of supervisors needs two-thirds voter approval to pass a special tax, an initiative proposing the identical tax can pass with a simple majority.
Proposition 43 would close that loophole for voter-proposed local special taxes approved after January 1, 2027.
Several tax increase proposals on this November’s ballot show why this protection is important for the future.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Election Day is here.
California voters are set to choose a new governor, vote on all other statewide offices and decide 14 propositions.

For this cycle, voters will also elect their U.S. representative using maps that were redrawn to favor Democrats. Californians adopted Proposition 50, which created maps using redrawn districts targeting five Republicans that in turn affected the boundaries of neighboring districts. The races could help decide the balance of power in Congress.
(See live coverage of Election Day starting at 4 a.m. PT in the video above.)
We'll keep updating this story with the latest information as Election Day unfolds.
What time do polls open and close on Election Day?
All California vote centers open Tuesday at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. for those who wish to vote in person or return their ballot there. Voters can also return their vote-by-mail ballot at secure dropbox locations.
California officials recommended that people who planned to mail their ballot get that done at least a week in advance. Mail must be postmarked on or before Nov. 3 to count.
Where can I find my polling place?
You can find a vote center on the back of your county voter information guide or by clicking here (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/polling-place).
The state is also offering a service where people can text "vote" to 468-683 (GOVOTE) to find their polling place.

What to know about the Election Day forecast
A cold front passing through will bring some periods of showers and Sierra snow across Northern California. Scattered showers should reach Sacramento and the surrounding area by late morning. Rain will start in the Foothills before noon. In the Sierra, expect rain and snow showers from midday into the early evening. See the full forecast here (https://www.kcra.com/article/northern-california-election-day-rain-snow-november-3/74313505).
Missed your voter registration date? California offers same-day registration
In California, the deadline to register to vote before an election is 15 days. However, if you miss the deadline, you can cast a ballot provisionally. California law states any voter whose qualifications cannot be immediately verified can cast a ballot provisionally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot.https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration/nvra/laws-standards/nvra-manual/chap-5#:~:text=California%20law%20provides%20that%20any,to%20cast%20a%20provisional%20ballot). This process involves comparing the signature of the provisional ballot with the signature on the voter's affidavit of registration to ensure the person is properly registered to vote.
California also allows for same-day registration until 8 p.m. on Election Day. You can sign up for conditional voter registration at your county elections office, or any vote center or polling place in your county.
Track your vote in California
The Secretary of State's Office offers a way for voters to track their ballot online (https://wheresmyballot.sos.ca.gov/). The service allows people to receive updates when their ballot is mailed, received, counted or if an issue comes up. Voters will have the option of email, text or phone call updates.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
The KCRA live updates page is dated Nov 3, 2026 and reads "Election Day is here," so the snapshot looks like it was taken on election day. Its "Voters begin casting ballots" and "Voters head to polls" lines suggest it may come from during the day. Still, I can't see any results in these pages.

I'm still not finding any results, so the vote may not have been counted or cached yet. I'll run a few more searches for Prop 43 results and vote counts from the next day, and I'll also look for more recent polling from other pollsters to get a better read on where it stands.

I'm comparing the poll numbers for Prop 43: PPIC has it at 42% yes and 55% no, while Berkeley IGS shows 36% yes and 46% no with a much larger undecided share. Undecided voters on ballot measures usually lean toward no, so that matters for where this is headed. I'm also recalling how other recent California measures that trailed in polls, like 2024 Prop 5 and 2022 Prop 30, ended up failing.

I'm recalling how past California tax measures fared, like the 2018 gas tax repeal, which failed despite early support. Measures polling under 45% often lose as the campaign goes on. I'm also weighing that the question is really whether Prop 43 passes, given the trailing numbers.

The two polls put Yes behind on both sides, by about 13 points in PPIC and 10 in Berkeley IGS, and the gap is wider than the undecided share could easily close. Yes would need roughly four in five of the undecided voters just to draw level in the Berkeley numbers, which looks very unlikely. The PPIC numbers leave almost no undecided room at all.

I'm weighing the broader picture here: polls for ballot measures can miss, but a 13-point deficit with three weeks left is hard to overcome. The "No" side usually gains as campaigns wear on, and I'm recalling that Prop 5 in 2024, which had a similar threshold-lowering theme, still failed by about ten points. The partisan split also matters, since Republicans lean strongly Yes while Democrats do not, and California's Democratic-leaning electorate pulls the result down.

I'm weighing the campaign finance too: the Yes side has about $15.3M against No's $7.9M, but labor and firefighter groups on the No side have a strong ground game. I'll also check whether the measure has major endorsements, since the party and several papers are against it even though the Legislature passed it with lopsided bipartisan votes.

I'm checking the newspaper editorial positions on Prop 43 next, including whether the Southern California News Group board backs Yes. Since I can't see results, I'm settling on a forecast from the polls and campaign dynamics, which points toward No winning. My working answer is that the Yes side is not the more likely outcome.

I'm weighing whether to answer "no" on the basis that the No side is ahead in the polls. The question's framing means "yes" points to the Yes side winning, so the polls suggest "no." I still want to check more polls and any post-election results before settling on that.

I'm checking for any later polls or late-campaign news on Prop 43, such as shifts in donors, Newsom's position, or the No side's ads. I'm also looking at how past California measures that tried to make tax approval harder, like the 2024 Prop 5 and the 2010 Prop 26, fared.

I'm checking the older California measures that tried to make tax approval harder, like Prop 39 in 2000, which passed with 57% for school bonds, and how Prop 6 in 2018 failed. Some tax-limiting measures have passed when framed as taxpayer protection, but the 2024 Prop 5 and Prop 32 results point the other way.

I'm weighing a couple of historical analogs: local special taxes often pass above two-thirds, but many land in the 55–65% range, so the precedent is mixed. The bigger factor is that the No side's "majority rule" message, plus labor opposition from teachers, firefighters, and SEIU, is persuasive to voters, while the polls show Yes flat or slipping.

I'm going to search for more Prop 43 polls, including Emerson and SurveyUSA, and look at how Republicans and Democrats are splitting on it.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.

Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).

Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)

Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.

A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.

When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Endorsement: Prop 43 is absurd, but so is California’s entire system of taxation
John Blanchard/S.F. Chronicle
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 23, 2026
Clocking in at barely over a paragraph, Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is the most straightforward measure on California’s November ballot.
It would mandate two-thirds voter approval (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop43-110326.pdf) — up from a simple majority — for local special taxes placed on the ballot by private citizens.
Sounds simple. But the story of how it got there involves decades-long legal battles and political bloodbaths befitting “Game of Thrones.”
Despite commanding far less attention (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-proposition-43-22465350.php) than Prop 40, the billionaire tax, Prop 43 is almost as controversial. At the heart of both measures is a legal, logistical and moral question reverberating throughout the nation (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/18/property-taxes-housing-affordability-issue-01105514?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e): Who should pay for government services, and how should those taxes work?

Article continues below this ad
While Prop 40 zeroes in on the state budget, Prop 43 focuses on how local governments raise money.
Understanding the measure requires going back to 1978, when voters approved Prop 13, the brainchild of anti-tax advocate Howard Jarvis. That measure put strict caps on property taxes — local governments’ main source of revenue.
The impact was immediate and devastating. Within the first year of Prop 13’s passage, city and county governments’ property tax revenue dropped by 60%, creating a $10 billion hole, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/3497).
Yet Prop 13 also made it more difficult for them to raise money in other ways by requiring two-thirds voter approval for local “special” taxes, which earmark funds for specific purposes. (General taxes, which don’t specify how money must be spent, can pass with a simple majority.)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Desperate to maintain core services such as police and fire departments — and daunted by the two-thirds threshold — local governments attempted to raise funds through assessments and property-related “fees.”
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association fought back. In 1996, voters approved the group’s Prop 218 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html), which made it harder for local governments to use those alternative methods.
So, to keep services running, California started picking up the tab.
Before Prop 13, local governments largely funded public education. Now, the state dedicates 40% of its budget to education. Yet with Prop 13 effectively choking off the most stable source of revenue — property taxes — California is forced to rely on income taxes from the wealthiest 1% of taxpayers, (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-taxes-proposition-3-22435509.php) which fluctuate wildly with the stock market.
With the perennial instability of state funding assistance, local governments are still struggling. Along with interest groups, they’ve repeatedly tried to punch holes in Prop 13.

Article continues below this ad
A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.

When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.

Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.

Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

The KCRA live updates page is dated Nov 3, 2026 and reads "Election Day is here," so the snapshot looks like it was taken on election day. Its "Voters begin casting ballots" and "Voters head to polls" lines suggest it may come from during the day. Still, I can't see any results in these pages.

I'm still not finding any results, so the vote may not have been counted or cached yet. I'll run a few more searches for Prop 43 results and vote counts from the next day, and I'll also look for more recent polling from other pollsters to get a better read on where it stands.

I'm comparing the poll numbers for Prop 43: PPIC has it at 42% yes and 55% no, while Berkeley IGS shows 36% yes and 46% no with a much larger undecided share. Undecided voters on ballot measures usually lean toward no, so that matters for where this is headed. I'm also recalling how other recent California measures that trailed in polls, like 2024 Prop 5 and 2022 Prop 30, ended up failing.

I'm recalling how past California tax measures fared, like the 2018 gas tax repeal, which failed despite early support. Measures polling under 45% often lose as the campaign goes on. I'm also weighing that the question is really whether Prop 43 passes, given the trailing numbers.

The two polls put Yes behind on both sides, by about 13 points in PPIC and 10 in Berkeley IGS, and the gap is wider than the undecided share could easily close. Yes would need roughly four in five of the undecided voters just to draw level in the Berkeley numbers, which looks very unlikely. The PPIC numbers leave almost no undecided room at all.

I'm weighing the broader picture here: polls for ballot measures can miss, but a 13-point deficit with three weeks left is hard to overcome. The "No" side usually gains as campaigns wear on, and I'm recalling that Prop 5 in 2024, which had a similar threshold-lowering theme, still failed by about ten points. The partisan split also matters, since Republicans lean strongly Yes while Democrats do not, and California's Democratic-leaning electorate pulls the result down.

I'm weighing the campaign finance too: the Yes side has about $15.3M against No's $7.9M, but labor and firefighter groups on the No side have a strong ground game. I'll also check whether the measure has major endorsements, since the party and several papers are against it even though the Legislature passed it with lopsided bipartisan votes.

I'm checking the newspaper editorial positions on Prop 43 next, including whether the Southern California News Group board backs Yes. Since I can't see results, I'm settling on a forecast from the polls and campaign dynamics, which points toward No winning. My working answer is that the Yes side is not the more likely outcome.

I'm weighing whether to answer "no" on the basis that the No side is ahead in the polls. The question's framing means "yes" points to the Yes side winning, so the polls suggest "no." I still want to check more polls and any post-election results before settling on that.

I'm checking for any later polls or late-campaign news on Prop 43, such as shifts in donors, Newsom's position, or the No side's ads. I'm also looking at how past California measures that tried to make tax approval harder, like the 2024 Prop 5 and the 2010 Prop 26, fared.

I'm checking the older California measures that tried to make tax approval harder, like Prop 39 in 2000, which passed with 57% for school bonds, and how Prop 6 in 2018 failed. Some tax-limiting measures have passed when framed as taxpayer protection, but the 2024 Prop 5 and Prop 32 results point the other way.

I'm weighing a couple of historical analogs: local special taxes often pass above two-thirds, but many land in the 55–65% range, so the precedent is mixed. The bigger factor is that the No side's "majority rule" message, plus labor opposition from teachers, firefighters, and SEIU, is persuasive to voters, while the polls show Yes flat or slipping.

I'm going to search for more Prop 43 polls, including Emerson and SurveyUSA, and look at how Republicans and Democrats are splitting on it.
