A major breakthrough occurred in 2017, when the California Supreme Court issued a ruling (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/CA-Supreme-Court-makes-it-a-bit-easier-for-tax-12112661.php), known as the Upland decision, that found the two-thirds voter approval requirement only applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. If private citizens gather signatures for a special local tax initiative, it only needs a simple majority to pass.
Suddenly, a new revenue pathway was open.
In 2018, 61% of San Francisco voters cast ballots in favor of Prop C, which taxed large businesses to fund homeless services. That was less than two-thirds, but because private citizens — not the Board of Supervisors — placed it on the ballot, the state Supreme Court cleared the city to spend the money (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/Calif-Supreme-Court-lets-2018-s-Prop-C-stand-15555452.php).
So, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association went to battle once again.
The group qualified a measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/21-0042A1%20%28Taxes%29.pdf) for the 2024 ballot that would have retroactively invalidated local special taxes that passed with less than a two-thirds vote. It would also have created additional layers of voter approvals for state and local taxes.

When the California Supreme Court reviewed the Jarvis measure (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/jerry-brown-ballot-18643109.php) at the behest of Democratic lawmakers, however, justices found it too far-reaching and yanked it from the ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/tax-ballot-measure-19520534.php).
So, Jarvis came back with a more tailored effort (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/measure-ula-howard-jarvis-ballot-mansion/) — this time backed by influential developers, businesses and real-estate groups.
It aimed to overturn the Upland ruling — and invalidate special taxes that had passed with less than a supermajority since 2017. It also proposed a strict cap on local transfer taxes — overriding those in 26 charter cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Staring at a multibillion-dollar budget crater for local governments, (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0006A1%29.pdf) Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, introduceda bill to constrain local transfer taxes (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab736), although not as stringently as the initiative would have. This appeased the developers who largely funded the measure.
But Jarvis refused to withdraw it. The group’s main priority, vice president of communications Susan Shelley told us, was reversing the Upland decision.

Ultimately, a deal was struck (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/).
Jarvis agreed to withdraw its measure — leaving transfer taxes intact — in exchange for lawmakers sending a replacement to the ballot that required all future citizen-led local special taxes to pass with a two-thirds supermajority. Lawmakers also withdrew their own ballot measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202320240aca13) — aimed at neutering Jarvis — that would have required any initiative mandating a two-thirds vote to itself be approved by two-thirds.
That is the head-spinning story of how we ended up with Prop 43.
So, how should voters evaluate this chimera of a measure?
On its face, it’s undemocratic to permit a minority of voters to block local special taxes supported by a majority.
At the same time, it’s hard to dispute that a lower threshold for private citizens has unleashed a wave of kooky measures with ripple effects that range from hamstringing legislators’ ability to close deficits to advancing horrible policy (see Prop I on San Francisco’s ballot (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-i-housing-san-francisco-22459341.php)).
Nor do we buy opponents’ argument that Prop 43 would be a death knell for local governments. Life existed in California before the 2017 Upland ruling. If a tax is needed and the plans are sound, voters will support it. Los Angeles County is building a multibillion-dollar transit system thanks to 2016’s Measure M, (https://www.metro.net/about/measure-m/) which passed with over 71% of the vote.
Moreover, consider the parcel tax on Oakland’s June ballot, which labor groups framed as existential for the city’s ability to fund firefighters and police officers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/oakland-tax-measure-e-22278781.php). When voters rejected the measure, the city still balanced its budget (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/oakland-measure-e-parcel-tax/) — and avoided closing fire stations — without the money.
Yet, dissatisfied with their existing salaries and benefits, thousands of Oakland city workers, including police and fire dispatchers, recently voted to go on strike (https://www.seiu1021.org/article/votes-are-we-have-voted-overwhelmingly-strike).
A similar situation is occurring in San Francisco. Even as Mayor Daniel Lurie warns of an impending doom loop for Muni if voters don’t approve the Prop H parcel tax (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-h-muni-san-francisco-22456325.php) in November, his administration offered city workers, including Muni drivers, 12% raises over the next four years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/sf-union-contracts-raise-city-workers-22422968.php), with a promise of no layoffs.
These examples point to an uncomfortable truth: Ballot measures are increasingly seen as cash grabs. Policymakers often feel they have no choice but to grant unsustainable salary increases and benefits — because they can pay for them with bottomless ballot campaigns.
Local governments would arguably benefit from the leverage Prop 43 would provide to keep spending in check.
Yet the measure is ultimately not a solution.
Prop 13 was intended to stymie unsustainable spending. But the budget instability it created, combined with California’s direct democracy and penchant for deceptive ballot measures (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-44-california-health-clinic-22433656.php), has created a monstrous, incoherent system of loopholes and backroom deals.
California is living in a mess of our own making. Whether or not Prop 43 passes is less significant than its mere existence.
We need comprehensive tax reform.
The states with the best outcomes — like Massachusetts — don’t have citizen tax measures. Local governments don’t need them because their states have built stable tax structures to maintain robust public services with reasonable restraints to ensure spending doesn’t get out of control.

We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either. If the measure passes, perhaps it will finally force California to build the coherent system of taxation we so clearly need.

When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times. The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.
The survey also found that a solid majority of likely voters opposed Proposition 39, which would require Californians to provide identification when voting and election officials to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens. The findings come as the Trump administration continues to attack California as a haven for voter fraud, including unfounded allegations of rampant illegal voting by undocumented immigrants.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Mark DiCamillo, the poll’s director, said previous surveys showed support for Proposition 40 has been fragile, and the most recent shows its prospects have dimmed as election day approaches.
The increase in opposition to Proposition 40 is “broad-based and spans virtually all major segments of the electorate,” DiCamillio said. The ballot measure was leading in a Berkeley poll conducted just six weeks ago, albeit by a slim margin, so its reversal of fortune is significant, he said.
Advertisement
The declining support comes after an onslaught of money spent opposing Proposition 40, including a torrent of television and social media ads airing everywhere from NFL games to “Everybody Loves Raymond” reruns. Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit. Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings. Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.
A plurality of voters oppose Propositions 41 and 42, a reversal from just six week ago, according to the poll.
In mid-September, voters were closely divided about Proposition 41 — 37% in favor and 33% opposed — (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/2zw023kt) with a large number of undecided. In the current poll, 38% of likely voters favor the measure and 47% oppose it. Proposition 42 led by 9 percentage points in the Berkeley/L.A. Times poll in September — 43% in favor and 34% opposed. Now, 43% of likely voters support it and 45% oppose it.
DiCamillo said backers of a ballot measure also should be concerned any time support registers below 50%, since voters who are undecided or unsure tend to vote no.
“It’s below 50%, and it’s trending down. Both of those are ominous signs,” DiCamillo said. Proposition 42 is “still very close. I’m not saying it’s definitely going down, but it’s moving in the wrong direction late in the campaign, and usually movement in a late poll is even more significant than the actual numbers themselves.”
He added that while many voters were unaware the two proposed ballot measures were designed as poison pills to kill the billionaire tax, among those who knew, the opposition was significantly greater.

Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
14 propositions that could remake California taxes, housing, healthcare and elections (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)
In addition to high-stakes U.S. House races, California voters in November also will weigh in on a slew of ballot measures.
July 6, 2026
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

ry for the billionaires who spent aggressively to tank the wealth tax.
Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

In addition to high-stakes U.S. House races, California voters in November also will weigh in on a slew of ballot measures.
July 6, 2026
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

I'm also thinking about how California ballot measures that poll this low this close to the vote usually fare, while noting that a less-known measure with a catchy "tax protection" message and a money edge could still defy the numbers.

I'm recalling how past California measures polled against their results: Prop 6 in 2018 polled in the low 40s and finished about the same, but Prop 22 in 2020 won with 58% despite polling below 50%, helped by heavy spending from Uber and Lyft.

I'm recalling how past California measures polled against their results, and Prop 22 in 2020 stands out: it won with a majority despite polling below 50%, helped by heavy late spending. I'm going back over past California measures that polled below 50% and finished close to those numbers, like Props 32, 27, 30, 29 and 26 from 2022 and 2024, along with Prop 15 in 2020. Several of those ended up failing, which makes the pattern the No side is running on look fairly strong.

I'm weighing the historical record here: California measures polling under 50% in the final weeks have mostly failed, with the 2020 Prop 22 win as a notable exception. The Yes side would need to move about eight points among No-leaning voters in roughly two weeks, which is a steep climb even with its current money edge.

Proposition 43
Should local tax measures placed on the ballot by voter signature face a higher threshold if the tax will be used for a specific purpose?
Proposition 43 would make it harder to pass new local tax measures by requiring a two-thirds vote to approve measures that earmark funds for a specific purpose, known as special taxes. Currently, special taxes proposed by cities, counties or special districts need that supermajority approval, but as a result of a 2017 California Supreme Court ruling, special taxes proposed by voters require only a majority vote.
Yes Argument
If a campaign wants to raise taxes for a specific purpose, it should have to win broad voter support. Allowing a lower threshold for tax measures placed on the ballot by voter signatures is a loophole that has added to the tax burden facing Californians. This measure will restore the higher threshold for passing special taxes at the local level that existed before the court chipped away at longstanding tax law.
No Argument
Local tax policy should not be governed by minority rule. One-third of voters should not be able to overrule the majority who are willing to raise taxes for important local services. City and county governments across California are facing tight budgets; now is not the time to limit their ability to stay afloat.

Prop. 43 Would Make It Harder to Raise Local Taxes. Can It Pass?
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, an anti-tax group who brought California the landmark Proposition 13, is now sponsoring Proposition 43 — a measure to make it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes.
Aug 18, 2026
Updated Oct 6, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
Listen
Close-up of ballot drop box outside of polling place
This November, California voters will consider Proposition 43 — a measure aimed at making it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes. It’s sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. That’s the anti-tax group that brought California Proposition 13 in 1978, a landmark ballot measure limiting property tax increases.
Marisa sits down with the President of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Jon Coupal. They discuss Prop. 43 and California’s broader tax system.
You can also listen to the Non-Profit Housing Association’s Bill Barnes explain the opposition (https://www.kqed.org/news/12103136/why-opponents-of-prop-43-say-it-would-cripple-local-funding) to Prop. 43.

Proposition 43
Should local tax measures placed on the ballot by voter signature face a higher threshold if the tax will be used for a specific purpose?
Proposition 43 would make it harder to pass new local tax measures by requiring a two-thirds vote to approve measures that earmark funds for a specific purpose, known as special taxes. Currently, special taxes proposed by cities, counties or special districts need that supermajority approval, but as a result of a 2017 California Supreme Court ruling, special taxes proposed by voters require only a majority vote.
Yes Argument
If a campaign wants to raise taxes for a specific purpose, it should have to win broad voter support. Allowing a lower threshold for tax measures placed on the ballot by voter signatures is a loophole that has added to the tax burden facing Californians. This measure will restore the higher threshold for passing special taxes at the local level that existed before the court chipped away at longstanding tax law.
No Argument
Local tax policy should not be governed by minority rule. One-third of voters should not be able to overrule the majority who are willing to raise taxes for important local services. City and county governments across California are facing tight budgets; now is not the time to limit their ability to stay afloat.

content.thinking:
I'm checking the Citrin-POLITICO poll dates and whether it included Prop 43. A Politico Playbook item lists Prop 43 alongside Prop 39 as trailing by double digits, and I need to work out whether that figure came from the PPIC survey or from a separate Politico story.

I'm now checking the Prop 43 numbers, which put it at 42-55 for a 13-point gap, and I'm weighing the KQED campaign finance totals as of Nov 1 against the earlier, smaller cash-on-hand figures from September. The Yes side's money looks concentrated in a few large donors, while the No side's spending is spread across labor groups.

I'm weighing the late polls, which put the No side clearly ahead, with Yes support below 50% and some voters still undecided. I'm also thinking about how California ballot measures that poll this low this close to the vote usually fare, while noting that a less-known measure with a catchy "tax protection" message and a money edge could still defy the numbers.

I'm recalling how past California measures polled against their results: Prop 6 in 2018 polled in the low 40s and finished about the same, but Prop 22 in 2020 won with 58% despite polling below 50%, helped by heavy spending from Uber and Lyft.

I'm recalling how past California measures polled against their results, and Prop 22 in 2020 stands out: it won with a majority despite polling below 50%, helped by heavy late spending. Several 2024 measures also show polls can understate or overstate support, with Prop 33 landing close to its polling and Prop 36 well above it.

I'm going back over past California measures that polled below 50% and finished close to those numbers, like Props 32, 27, 30, 29 and 26 from 2022 and 2024, along with Prop 15 in 2020. Several of those ended up failing, which makes the pattern the No side is running on look fairly strong.

I'm weighing the historical record here: California measures polling under 50% in the final weeks have mostly failed, with the 2020 Prop 22 win as a notable exception. The Yes side would need to move about eight points among No-leaning voters in roughly two weeks, which is a steep climb even with its current money edge.

I'm estimating the likely-voter mix, roughly 45% Democratic, 25% Republican, and 30% independent or other, and weighting each group's yes share to see where the overall number lands.

I'm checking whether the Democratic Party's official stance on Prop 43 lines up with how Democratic voters are leaning in the polls, since the Legislature's near-unanimous vote for ACA 22 makes that relationship look less clear-cut.

I'm working out how to read the yes/no format: a "which side" question answered with only yes or no implies a yes/no framing, so I need to pick the most natural one, likely whether the No side is the one more likely to win.

I'm settling on "no" as the answer, reading the question as whether the Yes side will win, so "no" means the No side is more likely to prevail. I'm also wondering if the election has already happened, since my searches haven't turned up any results yet.

I'm checking whether any post-election results for Prop 43 have come out, searching a few different phrasings like "voters approve" or "voters reject." I'm also planning to look for late campaign moves from the Yes side and the No side's opposition ads, plus the state Democratic Party's official position.

I'm checking the remaining search angles for Prop 43, looking for any sign that results are already out.

Proposition 43
Should local tax measures placed on the ballot by voter signature face a higher threshold if the tax will be used for a specific purpose?
Proposition 43 would make it harder to pass new local tax measures by requiring a two-thirds vote to approve measures that earmark funds for a specific purpose, known as special taxes. Currently, special taxes proposed by cities, counties or special districts need that supermajority approval, but as a result of a 2017 California Supreme Court ruling, special taxes proposed by voters require only a majority vote.
Yes Argument
If a campaign wants to raise taxes for a specific purpose, it should have to win broad voter support. Allowing a lower threshold for tax measures placed on the ballot by voter signatures is a loophole that has added to the tax burden facing Californians. This measure will restore the higher threshold for passing special taxes at the local level that existed before the court chipped away at longstanding tax law.
No Argument
Local tax policy should not be governed by minority rule. One-third of voters should not be able to overrule the majority who are willing to raise taxes for important local services. City and county governments across California are facing tight budgets; now is not the time to limit their ability to stay afloat.

This November, California voters will consider Proposition 43 — a measure aimed at making it harder for cities and counties to raise local taxes. I'm noting that KQED lists the California Republican Party, the California Taxpayers Association, and HJTA as key supporters, with the California Democratic Party, the State Association of Counties, and SEIU California opposing. So the Yes side has the state GOP behind it, and the No side has the Democrats, counties, and SEIU. Bay Area officials are sounding the alarm over a lesser-known California ballot measure
Kathryn Palmer
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 12:00 PM UTC
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee appear alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 in San Francisco on Oct. 7, 2026. (Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle)
It's not often that the supporters and opponents of a ballot measure agree on what exactly it would do, let alone describe it the same way. Yet both sides of the fight over Proposition 43 have been clear: It will make it harder to raise local taxes.
What they don't agree on is whether it's a good idea.
Bay Area leaders last week joined a growing chorus of local government officials across the state voicing strong opposition to Proposition 43, slamming the measure as a threat to critical financial lifelines for cities and counties.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday also said he plans to vote against Prop 43, siding with a wide collection of Democratic lawmakers and local government officials who oppose the measure.
Supporters, led by the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that as the state and nation grapple with an affordability crisis, raising taxes should be difficult.
General taxes, which aren't earmarked for a specific use and go into a city's general fund, can pass with a simple majority. But taxes that will go toward a specific purpose - like pay raises for police and fire personnel, or homeless services - are subject to a much higher two-thirds vote requirement when they're placed on the ballot by government officials.
This puts anyone looking to raise revenue in a strange bind: Voters are much more likely to support a tax increase when they know it's going to fix a specific problem. They're less likely to OK a general tax hike that could fund virtually anything. Yet the two-thirds requirement is a significant hurdle, making it almost impossible to raise special taxes.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Prop 43 would extend that two-thirds threshold to special tax measures placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives, not just those spearheaded by government officials. It would mean all special taxes would need to be approved by a much higher percentage of voters than other ballot measures.
Local leaders across California, including many in the Bay Area, have begun sounding the alarm over the implications if Prop 43 were to pass.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee joined San Francisco Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and representatives of housing and public safety groups last week to urge voters to reject the measure, warning it would hamstring communities' ability to raise funds for local needs. They also warned it would enhance the veto power of a select few, potentially inviting "special interests" to try to sway election outcomes.
"Prop 43 undermines democracy by upending majority rule, making it harder for communities across California to support first responders, parks, libraries and affordable housing," Lurie said at a press conference in San Francisco last week. "Voters know what our communities need to keep our neighborhoods safe, keep Muni moving, and build more housing."
Advertisement
Advertisement
Supporters have cast the court decisions allowing citizens' special tax initiatives to pass by simple majority as a loophole. If Prop 43 passes, it would essentially hit the rewind button to a period before a 2017 state Supreme Court decision led to the current simple majority rule.
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association spokesperson Susan Shelley said local governments would still be able to pass general tax increases by a simple majority under Prop 43, and argued local officials should prioritize their budgets to pay for essential services first.
"Proposition 43 makes it harder to raise taxes, like sales taxes," Shelley said. "It restores the requirement for a two-thirds vote of the people if the money from a local tax will be earmarked and locked for a special purpose."
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee appear alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 in San Francisco on Oct. 7, 2026. (Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle)
The ballot measure also counts Reform California as a supporter, the campaign group helmed by firebrand GOP Assembly Member Carl DeMaio.
Advertisement
Advertisement
The California Republican Party, along with some Republican lawmakers and a few current and former Bay Area officials, back the measure. The list includes Debora Allen, former BART director, and Quentin Kopp, former San Francisco supervisor.
The coalition of those fighting Prop 43 got a boost last week when Newsom endorsed a no vote, a position in lockstep with the California Democratic Party, several prominent Democratic state and local lawmakers and associations representing California cities and counties.
The League of California Cities opposes Prop 43, as does the California State Association of Counties and the California Special Districts Association, collectively representing hundreds municipalities across the state.
Susan Ellenberg, president of the California State Association of Counties, said in a statement to the Chronicle that many local needs depend on community-driven funding, such as wildfire prevention, emergency response and behavioral health.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"The measure would also limit residents' ability to propose and approve solutions through the initiative process, even when those solutions earn broad majority support," said Ellenberg, who is also a Santa Clara County supervisor. "For local governments already facing strained budgets and increasing responsibilities, this change would reshape how communities address their most pressing priorities."
Ellenberg and other Santa Clara County leaders backed a 2024 tax increase that they billed as a measure to fund healthcare services in the wake of Trump administration cuts. But Measure A was a general tax increase, subject to the much lower vote threshold, meaning the money can technically be spent on anything. It passed with 57% of the vote.
As of Tuesday, the Yes on 43 campaign has a slight financial edge, banking more than $10 million in campaign funds so far. The anti-43 campaign reported just under $8 million.
In 2024, eight special sales tax measures qualified for local ballots across the state by a citizens initiative, ranging from a ¼ cent to 1 cent increase. Of the four that passed with a simple majority, none met Prop 43's 2/3 vote threshold. The two that received the most support were Sonoma County's Measure I to fund child care and Benicia's Measure F to fund road improvements. They both passed at 62% and 61%, respectively.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Other prominent special tax measures include the Los Angeles mansion tax, which voters passed by majority in 2022 and places a 4% tax on real estate sales on multimillion-dollar homes.
Prop 43 arose out of a deal cut to avoid another qualified ballot measure from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association that took aim at elements of the mansion tax.
It was that last-minute legislative brokering that led the anti-tax group to instead put forward Prop 43, with the help of Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. Soon after Prop 43 qualified for the November ballot, Wicks disavowed it, calling it "the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot."
Isaac Martin, a sociology professor at UC San Diego who has written multiple books about taxation and public finance, described Prop 43 as affecting a goldilocks-like subset of tax measures: popular enough for a simple majority, but not popular enough to pass overwhelmingly.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"Since it would make it harder for local governments to raise money for popular services, the options are to raise funds for general government, including popular and less popular services, or do without," Martin said. "I mean, bottom line, those are sort of the only options for local governments."
Groups that oppose the measure argue the new threshold would make it harder for communities to make hyper-specific funding decisions to tackle local priorities.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters advocacy group representing thousands of firefighters, said the measure risks cutting off crucial public safety funding. He pointed to Measure H in Sonoma County and Measure E in Los Angeles County, both passed by voters in 2024. The taxes both raise funds to bolster the two counties' fire protection and emergency response services - top priorities in regions that have been devastated by some of the state's deadliest wildfires in recent years.
"Any time you have local elected leaders, public safety and community advocates, or people that are running local health clinics or infrastructure projects, say that they need to get something done in their community, it should be the community that decides, with a simple majority," Roberts said.

Bay Area officials are sounding the alarm over a lesser-known California ballot measure
Kathryn Palmer
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 12:00 PM UTC
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee appear alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 in San Francisco on Oct. 7, 2026. (Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle)
It's not often that the supporters and opponents of a ballot measure agree on what exactly it would do, let alone describe it the same way. Yet both sides of the fight over Proposition 43 have been clear: It will make it harder to raise local taxes.
What they don't agree on is whether it's a good idea.
Bay Area leaders last week joined a growing chorus of local government officials across the state voicing strong opposition to Proposition 43, slamming the measure as a threat to critical financial lifelines for cities and counties.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday also said he plans to vote against Prop 43, siding with a wide collection of Democratic lawmakers and local government officials who oppose the measure.
Supporters, led by the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that as the state and nation grapple with an affordability crisis, raising taxes should be difficult.
General taxes, which aren't earmarked for a specific use and go into a city's general fund, can pass with a simple majority. But taxes that will go toward a specific purpose - like pay raises for police and fire personnel, or homeless services - are subject to a much higher two-thirds vote requirement when they're placed on the ballot by government officials.
This puts anyone looking to raise revenue in a strange bind: Voters are much more likely to support a tax increase when they know it's going to fix a specific problem. They're less likely to OK a general tax hike that could fund virtually anything. Yet the two-thirds requirement is a significant hurdle, making it almost impossible to raise special taxes.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Prop 43 would extend that two-thirds threshold to special tax measures placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives, not just those spearheaded by government officials. It would mean all special taxes would need to be approved by a much higher percentage of voters than other ballot measures.
Local leaders across California, including many in the Bay Area, have begun sounding the alarm over the implications if Prop 43 were to pass.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee joined San Francisco Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and representatives of housing and public safety groups last week to urge voters to reject the measure, warning it would hamstring communities' ability to raise funds for local needs. They also warned it would enhance the veto power of a select few, potentially inviting "special interests" to try to sway election outcomes.
"Prop 43 undermines democracy by upending majority rule, making it harder for communities across California to support first responders, parks, libraries and affordable housing," Lurie said at a press conference in San Francisco last week. "Voters know what our communities need to keep our neighborhoods safe, keep Muni moving, and build more housing."
Advertisement
Advertisement
Supporters have cast the court decisions allowing citizens' special tax initiatives to pass by simple majority as a loophole. If Prop 43 passes, it would essentially hit the rewind button to a period before a 2017 state Supreme Court decision led to the current simple majority rule.
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association spokesperson Susan Shelley said local governments would still be able to pass general tax increases by a simple majority under Prop 43, and argued local officials should prioritize their budgets to pay for essential services first.
"Proposition 43 makes it harder to raise taxes, like sales taxes," Shelley said. "It restores the requirement for a two-thirds vote of the people if the money from a local tax will be earmarked and locked for a special purpose."
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee appear alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 in San Francisco on Oct. 7, 2026. (Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle)
The ballot measure also counts Reform California as a supporter, the campaign group helmed by firebrand GOP Assembly Member Carl DeMaio.
Advertisement
Advertisement
The California Republican Party, along with some Republican lawmakers and a few current and former Bay Area officials, back the measure. The list includes Debora Allen, former BART director, and Quentin Kopp, former San Francisco supervisor.
The coalition of those fighting Prop 43 got a boost last week when Newsom endorsed a no vote, a position in lockstep with the California Democratic Party, several prominent Democratic state and local lawmakers and associations representing California cities and counties.
The League of California Cities opposes Prop 43, as does the California State Association of Counties and the California Special Districts Association, collectively representing hundreds municipalities across the state.
Susan Ellenberg, president of the California State Association of Counties, said in a statement to the Chronicle that many local needs depend on community-driven funding, such as wildfire prevention, emergency response and behavioral health.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"The measure would also limit residents' ability to propose and approve solutions through the initiative process, even when those solutions earn broad majority support," said Ellenberg, who is also a Santa Clara County supervisor. "For local governments already facing strained budgets and increasing responsibilities, this change would reshape how communities address their most pressing priorities."
Ellenberg and other Santa Clara County leaders backed a 2024 tax increase that they billed as a measure to fund healthcare services in the wake of Trump administration cuts. But Measure A was a general tax increase, subject to the much lower vote threshold, meaning the money can technically be spent on anything. It passed with 57% of the vote.
As of Tuesday, the Yes on 43 campaign has a slight financial edge, banking more than $10 million in campaign funds so far. The anti-43 campaign reported just under $8 million.
In 2024, eight special sales tax measures qualified for local ballots across the state by a citizens initiative, ranging from a ¼ cent to 1 cent increase. Of the four that passed with a simple majority, none met Prop 43's 2/3 vote threshold. The two that received the most support were Sonoma County's Measure I to fund child care and Benicia's Measure F to fund road improvements. They both passed at 62% and 61%, respectively.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Other prominent special tax measures include the Los Angeles mansion tax, which voters passed by majority in 2022 and places a 4% tax on real estate sales on multimillion-dollar homes.
Prop 43 arose out of a deal cut to avoid another qualified ballot measure from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association that took aim at elements of the mansion tax.
It was that last-minute legislative brokering that led the anti-tax group to instead put forward Prop 43, with the help of Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. Soon after Prop 43 qualified for the November ballot, Wicks disavowed it, calling it "the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot."
Isaac Martin, a sociology professor at UC San Diego who has written multiple books about taxation and public finance, described Prop 43 as affecting a goldilocks-like subset of tax measures: popular enough for a simple majority, but not popular enough to pass overwhelmingly.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"Since it would make it harder for local governments to raise money for popular services, the options are to raise funds for general government, including popular and less popular services, or do without," Martin said. "I mean, bottom line, those are sort of the only options for local governments."
Groups that oppose the measure argue the new threshold would make it harder for communities to make hyper-specific funding decisions to tackle local priorities.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters advocacy group representing thousands of firefighters, said the measure risks cutting off crucial public safety funding. He pointed to Measure H in Sonoma County and Measure E in Los Angeles County, both passed by voters in 2024. The taxes both raise funds to bolster the two counties' fire protection and emergency response services - top priorities in regions that have been devastated by some of the state's deadliest wildfires in recent years.
"Any time you have local elected leaders, public safety and community advocates, or people that are running local health clinics or infrastructure projects, say that they need to get something done in their community, it should be the community that decides, with a simple majority," Roberts said.

I'm noting that KQED lists the California Republican Party, the California Taxpayers Association, and HJTA as key supporters, with the California Democratic Party, the State Association of Counties, and SEIU California opposing. So the Yes side has the state GOP behind it, and the No side has the Democrats, counties, and SEIU. I'm unsure whether the League of California Cities is involved, and I'll skip checking the Chamber of Commerce since it isn't needed.

I'm weighing the partisan split: Republicans lean yes and Democrats lean no, and since Democrats hold a large registration edge in California, a measure with that alignment usually struggles unless independents swing toward yes. I'm also thinking through past propositions like Prop 6 and Prop 22, and how Prop 26 in 2010 passed narrowly despite similar tax-limit themes.

I'm checking the PPIC final poll, which has Yes at 42 and No at 55, and estimating that Yes would need a net swing of about 13 points in the last two weeks to win. Late swings that large are uncommon in California, and they usually favor the status quo, so I'm treating that as a steep climb.

I'm recalling the Prop 22 polling from 2020, which had Yes ahead around 49 to 51 percent before finishing at 58.6, so late gains for a well-funded measure do happen. I'm also noting that Prop 19 in 2010 was polling near 47 percent and then lost, which shows the same kind of close number can go either way.

I'm recalling how recent California propositions polled against their final results, like Prop 36 in 2024, which polled high and passed comfortably, and Prop 33, which polled in the high 30s and failed. I'm also checking whether Prop 5 and Prop 32 followed a similar pattern, with support sliding late in the campaign.

I'm comparing recent California propositions against their polling: Prop 35 in 2024 polled around 55 and passed with 67, while Prop 30 in 2022 polled near 39 and finished at 42 and failed. I'm also recalling Prop 15 in 2020, which polled around 46 and ended at 48, still short.

I'm going back through the past propositions with their final polling against results, from Prop 16 in 2020, which polled around 43 and failed, to Prop 6 in 2018, which polled around 40 and ended at 43. I'm also noting Prop 10 that same year, which stayed near 40 and failed, while the 2018 housing bond and the 2016 cigarette tax and income tax extension both passed.

I'm checking the 2008 and 2010 measures against the polling, and the pattern holds: tax measures polling below 40 almost always fail, those in the mid-40s are close to a coin flip, and Prop 43 at 42 in PPIC and 36 in IGS sits in the unfavorable range. I'm also weighing the partisan split, where the Yes side is strong among Republicans but weak among Democrats, which doesn't point to a late surge.

I'm thinking about whether the Prop 43 Independent VoterProject survey, which found voters split with 40% in favor, changes the picture much. I'm also wondering whether there's a Politico/Citrin poll specifically on this measure that my earlier search didn't surface.

I'm checking whether the Desert Sun's poll numbers were about Prop 43 or a different measure, since that passage looked like it belonged to the billionaire tax. I'll also search for an Independent Voter Project survey, plus Emerson and SurveyUSA polls, to see if any of them tested Prop 43 directly.

I'm going to search for any Mason-Dixon or Target Insyght polls on Prop 43 as well.

It's not often that the supporters and opponents of a ballot measure agree on what exactly it would do, let alone describe it the same way. Yet both sides of the fight over Proposition 43 have been clear: It will make it harder to raise local taxes.
What they don't agree on is whether it's a good idea.
Bay Area leaders last week joined a growing chorus of local government officials across the state voicing strong opposition to Proposition 43, slamming the measure as a threat to critical financial lifelines for cities and counties.

Gov. Gavin Newsom on Friday also said he plans to vote against Prop 43, siding with a wide collection of Democratic lawmakers and local government officials who oppose the measure.
Supporters, led by the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that as the state and nation grapple with an affordability crisis, raising taxes should be difficult.
General taxes, which aren't earmarked for a specific use and go into a city's general fund, can pass with a simple majority. But taxes that will go toward a specific purpose - like pay raises for police and fire personnel, or homeless services - are subject to a much higher two-thirds vote requirement when they're placed on the ballot by government officials.
This puts anyone looking to raise revenue in a strange bind: Voters are much more likely to support a tax increase when they know it's going to fix a specific problem. They're less likely to OK a general tax hike that could fund virtually anything. Yet the two-thirds requirement is a significant hurdle, making it almost impossible to raise special taxes.
