Prop 43 would extend that two-thirds threshold to special tax measures placed on the ballot by citizen initiatives, not just those spearheaded by government officials. It would mean all special taxes would need to be approved by a much higher percentage of voters than other ballot measures.
Local leaders across California, including many in the Bay Area, have begun sounding the alarm over the implications if Prop 43 were to pass.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee joined San Francisco Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and representatives of housing and public safety groups last week to urge voters to reject the measure, warning it would hamstring communities' ability to raise funds for local needs. They also warned it would enhance the veto power of a select few, potentially inviting "special interests" to try to sway election outcomes.
"Prop 43 undermines democracy by upending majority rule, making it harder for communities across California to support first responders, parks, libraries and affordable housing," Lurie said at a press conference in San Francisco last week. "Voters know what our communities need to keep our neighborhoods safe, keep Muni moving, and build more housing."
Advertisement
Advertisement
Supporters have cast the court decisions allowing citizens' special tax initiatives to pass by simple majority as a loophole. If Prop 43 passes, it would essentially hit the rewind button to a period before a 2017 state Supreme Court decision led to the current simple majority rule.
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association spokesperson Susan Shelley said local governments would still be able to pass general tax increases by a simple majority under Prop 43, and argued local officials should prioritize their budgets to pay for essential services first.
"Proposition 43 makes it harder to raise taxes, like sales taxes," Shelley said. "It restores the requirement for a two-thirds vote of the people if the money from a local tax will be earmarked and locked for a special purpose."
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee appear alongside first responders to oppose Proposition 43 outside of Fire Station No. 5 in San Francisco on Oct. 7, 2026. (Weston Turtle Fudge/S.F. Chronicle)
The ballot measure also counts Reform California as a supporter, the campaign group helmed by firebrand GOP Assembly Member Carl DeMaio.
Advertisement
Advertisement
The California Republican Party, along with some Republican lawmakers and a few current and former Bay Area officials, back the measure. The list includes Debora Allen, former BART director, and Quentin Kopp, former San Francisco supervisor.
The coalition of those fighting Prop 43 got a boost last week when Newsom endorsed a no vote, a position in lockstep with the California Democratic Party, several prominent Democratic state and local lawmakers and associations representing California cities and counties.
The League of California Cities opposes Prop 43, as does the California State Association of Counties and the California Special Districts Association, collectively representing hundreds municipalities across the state.
Susan Ellenberg, president of the California State Association of Counties, said in a statement to the Chronicle that many local needs depend on community-driven funding, such as wildfire prevention, emergency response and behavioral health.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"The measure would also limit residents' ability to propose and approve solutions through the initiative process, even when those solutions earn broad majority support," said Ellenberg, who is also a Santa Clara County supervisor. "For local governments already facing strained budgets and increasing responsibilities, this change would reshape how communities address their most pressing priorities."
Ellenberg and other Santa Clara County leaders backed a 2024 tax increase that they billed as a measure to fund healthcare services in the wake of Trump administration cuts. But Measure A was a general tax increase, subject to the much lower vote threshold, meaning the money can technically be spent on anything. It passed with 57% of the vote.
As of Tuesday, the Yes on 43 campaign has a slight financial edge, banking more than $10 million in campaign funds so far. The anti-43 campaign reported just under $8 million.
In 2024, eight special sales tax measures qualified for local ballots across the state by a citizens initiative, ranging from a ¼ cent to 1 cent increase. Of the four that passed with a simple majority, none met Prop 43's 2/3 vote threshold. The two that received the most support were Sonoma County's Measure I to fund child care and Benicia's Measure F to fund road improvements. They both passed at 62% and 61%, respectively.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Other prominent special tax measures include the Los Angeles mansion tax, which voters passed by majority in 2022 and places a 4% tax on real estate sales on multimillion-dollar homes.
Prop 43 arose out of a deal cut to avoid another qualified ballot measure from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association that took aim at elements of the mansion tax.
It was that last-minute legislative brokering that led the anti-tax group to instead put forward Prop 43, with the help of Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland. Soon after Prop 43 qualified for the November ballot, Wicks disavowed it, calling it "the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot."
Isaac Martin, a sociology professor at UC San Diego who has written multiple books about taxation and public finance, described Prop 43 as affecting a goldilocks-like subset of tax measures: popular enough for a simple majority, but not popular enough to pass overwhelmingly.
Advertisement
Advertisement
"Since it would make it harder for local governments to raise money for popular services, the options are to raise funds for general government, including popular and less popular services, or do without," Martin said. "I mean, bottom line, those are sort of the only options for local governments."
Groups that oppose the measure argue the new threshold would make it harder for communities to make hyper-specific funding decisions to tackle local priorities.
Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters advocacy group representing thousands of firefighters, said the measure risks cutting off crucial public safety funding. He pointed to Measure H in Sonoma County and Measure E in Los Angeles County, both passed by voters in 2024. The taxes both raise funds to bolster the two counties' fire protection and emergency response services - top priorities in regions that have been devastated by some of the state's deadliest wildfires in recent years.
"Any time you have local elected leaders, public safety and community advocates, or people that are running local health clinics or infrastructure projects, say that they need to get something done in their community, it should be the community that decides, with a simple majority," Roberts said.

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? 5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/), CalMatters October 23, 2026 October 23, 2026

California voters are being asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.
Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).

Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. 5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/), CalMatters October 23, 2026 October 23, 2026

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
California voters are being asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.
Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).

This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).

Photo by Allen J. Schaben, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images In summary The measure would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special taxes, instead of the simple majority for citizen-led initiatives. Anti-tax advocates say it should be that hard for governments to tax Californians, but local officials say it could constrain funding for essential services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. In 2022, 58% of Los Angeles city voters approved a hefty tax on mansion sales. In 2024, 62% of Sonoma County voters backed a half-cent sales tax to fund wildfire response and other emergency services. Neither would have become law under the threshold set by Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/), which would require a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax measures that pay for specific services. Anti-tax advocates such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which helped get Prop. 43 on the ballot, say it should be harder (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) to tax Californians in a state where tax rates are already high. They argue that the measure would apply an equal standard to whoever wants a special tax, whether the government or citizen groups. Californians voted in 1996 (https://lao.ca.gov/1996/120196_prop_218/understanding_prop218_1296.html) to establish a two-thirds threshold for special tax measures. For decades, it was widely assumed that the threshold applied to all special taxes — until 2017, when the state Supreme Court said (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2017/08/state-supreme-court-made-easier-raise-taxes/) the law specifically applied only to tax measures put on the ballot by local officials. But what about special taxes proposed by citizens? The court declined to clarify (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/). Confusion ensued. Since then, several high-profile local special tax measures placed on the ballot by nongovernmental groups have passed with a simple majority. Local government officials, labor unions and affordable housing advocates oppose the measure, arguing the proposal would make it difficult to collect revenues for essential services, such as firefighting, education and healthcare. They argue it would allow “minority rule (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-43-taxes-minority-rule/)” because it would only take a third of voters to block special taxes. Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said Prop. 43 would clarify that the two-thirds rule applies to all special taxes. He said that the two-thirds vote requirement dates to the 1849 state Constitution, which required a supermajority vote of state lawmakers to ask voters to borrow money. “The power to tax is (the) government’s most draconian power,” he told CalMatters. “The people of the state of California have made it a policy that when you are going to exercise that power, it should require a higher degree of consensus.” But opponents say the initiative risks kneecapping funding for local services. Darrell Roberts, president of the California Professional Firefighters union, which represents 38,000 firefighters, called Prop. 43 an insurmountable roadblock (https://www.marinij.com/2026/10/03/opinion-prop-43-sacrifices-local-public-safety-to-protect-corporate-profits/) to raising money for community services. This November, Los Angeles voters will decide on a half-cent sales tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-06/lapd-union-will-oppose-half-cent-sales-tax-hike-pushed-by-firefighters-union) proposal to hire more firefighters, Roberts noted. “Under Prop. 43, it’s clear that the powerful few would be protected at the expense of everyone else,” he wrote in the Marin Independent Journal. Supporters have poured almost $15 million into the measure, nearly $10 million of it from the California Business Roundtable PAC. Opponents have collected $6 million, with the biggest contribution, $1.5 million, from a PAC affiliated with the Service Employees International Union of California. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 43 originated from L.A.’s ‘mansion tax’ fight Prop. 43 stems from a bitter fight over Los Angeles’ “mansion tax,” a 4% tax on real estate sales of more than $5.3 million and 5.5% on sales more than $10.6 million. The tax rates rise with inflation. It has generated $1.4 billion (https://housing.lacity.gov/ula-revenue) in revenue since it became law in 2023, according to the city. The tax angered real estate developers (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/04/proposition-realty-mansion-tax-jarvis/) and business groups, who said it impeded new construction of all kinds of developments, including affordable housing. The opposition fueled a campaign led by Coupal’s group earlier this year to qualify a ballot measure that would have slashed real estate sales taxes statewide, applied the two-thirds vote requirement to all special taxes and revoked taxes that previously passed by a simple majority, such as the mansion tax. Prop. 43 is a more modest proposal resulting from an eleventh-hour negotiation between Coupal and Democratic leaders in the state Legislature to kill the more extensive version. Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat, authored the compromise language (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca22). The measure is limited to the vote threshold and does not apply retroactively to taxes such as the mansion tax. Just days after the Legislature placed Prop. 43 on the ballot, Wicks said she is “adamantly opposed” to it. “The clock was running out, and we had a choice to make: Leave a retroactive measure on the ballot that threatened billions in local funding, or accept a much narrower constitutional amendment that I still believed was bad policy,” Wicks said (https://bsky.app/profile/buffywicks.bsky.social/post/3mpi3t4tkmp2h) in a social media post. Is there public appetite? This isn’t Coupal’s first rodeo. In 2024, his group sponsored a much broader ballot measure to make it harder to raise taxes, but the California Supreme Court unanimously blocked (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/) it before the election, deeming it an illegal attempt to change the state’s constitution. How will a narrower Prop. 43 perform this year? A September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California found 51% of likely voters would vote no on Prop. 43, versus just 43% who would vote yes. But Coupal hopes the proposal taps into voters’ concerns about affordability and their frustration with the high cost of living in California. “We are in a general climate right now where Californians really feel overtaxed,” he said. “California needs to prioritize its spending before it asks for more.” READ NEXT Why are out-of-state billionaires funding a California voter ID measure? 5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/), CalMatters October 23, 2026 October 23, 2026

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
California voters are being asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.
Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).

Photos by Fred Greaves and Rahul Lal for CalMatters In summary Polls have for months widely favored Democrat Xavier Becerra for governor in the most populous Democratic state in the country. Republican Steve Hilton is banking on dissatisfaction with the cost of living to get independents and even some liberals to consider him. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Californians are choosing their next governor: a longtime liberal politician pitching his government experience or a Republican first-time candidate vowing to dramatically upend Democratic power structures. The race between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom is one of the most consequential on the ballot. Polls for months have put Becerra ahead of Hilton by double digits, a predictable lead in a state with nearly twice as many registered Democrats as Republicans and where a Republican hasn’t won a statewide office in nearly two decades. Hilton, a former Fox News host (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/california-governor-hilton-profile/) who has urged voters to end “16 years of one-party rule,” is banking on frustration with the state’s high cost of living to drive undecided voters, independents and even some Democrats to support a Republican for a change. He represents the best hope in years for a GOP victory. He has raised more than $33 million to Becerra’s $38 million and is running hard on a series of ambitious promises to lower costs by slashing regulations and taxes. He portrayed Becerra as the embodiment of the California political status quo, someone who would make decisions that benefit influential special interest groups like organized labor. “It’s the people against the machine,” he said of his campaign in a virtual town hall last week. His message of change, promises to slash gas prices and frequent invocations of Californians moving out-of-state resonated with Brad Gerig, who voted in Roseville last week. It was the first time Gerig, 34, could recall voting for a Republican, he said. The EMT and firefighter said he wants to be able to afford to stay and raise a family in California, so he was willing to “try something different.” “I think it’s worth a shot,” Gerig said. “I think for everybody living in this area there’s an inherent angst for a little bit better. There’s no reason it should be as expensive as it is.” ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know But Hilton has struggled to rid himself of the baggage from President Donald Trump’s endorsement in a state Trump lost by 20 percentage points in 2024. Becerra has reminded voters of Hilton’s link to Trump at every turn, and cast himself as a fighter who would, like Newsom, challenge decisions in Washington such as Trump’s aggressive deportation campaign. He has dismissed Hilton as unserious and primarily campaigned on his longtime experience (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/california-governor-becerra-profile-promises/) representing Los Angeles in Congress and serving as state attorney general and as U.S. health secretary. Those roles have earned him a wide swath of influential liberal allies. “Xavier Becerra has stood with us for more than 30 years,” said Tony Hoang, executive director of the LGBTQ+ rights organization Equality California, at an event in San Francisco last week. Sign up for free Δ He highlighted Becerra’s role as one of the small minority of congressmembers who voted against the anti-gay marriage Defense of Marriage Act in 1996. At the same event, Becerra touted his opposition to Trump. “Donald Trump is on this ballot,” he said, without naming his opponent once. “We see right through you, Donald Trump. And we see through all those MAGA friends and relatives who are trying to push that agenda on us.” Becerra’s comfortable standing is reflected in the relatively muted nature of his campaign: Becerra agreed to meet for only one debate (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/09/california-general-election-gubernatorial-debate-cnn/) with Hilton this fall. He has spent much of his time campaigning not for himself but against a Republican-backed voter ID measure (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-39-voter-id/) and on behalf of other California Democrats. The election comes at a particularly delicate time for California. Street homelessness rose for years and only began to decline again in 2025. Wildfires have made it harder to buy homeowners insurance. Inflation, much of it attributable to Trump’s warin Iran, tariffs and immigration crackdown, have added to the already-high cost of living. The state budget, always subject to the boom and bust of the stock market, has become particularly dependent on the fortunes of the artificial intelligence industry. Under Newsom, the state has made aggressive regulatory moves to curb the use of climate-warming fossil fuels. But despite recent polling that shows a majority of Californians support the green transition, fewer are willing to pay higher prices (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) for energy than were a decade ago. And the state’s liberal politics have often put it in the crosshairs of the Trump administration, which has withheld federal funds, challenged California’s environmental policies and attempted to intervene in this election. Both candidates agree the state has become unaffordable for working families. That’s about all they agree on. Becerra has proposed mostly incremental changes to existing state policies, such as continuing recent efforts by Newsom and lawmakers to reduce the bureaucratic hurdles to approving new housing construction. He wants to expand state mortgage assistance programs and said he’s committed to the clean energy transition, but open to delays or tweaks to trim costs. He has not endorsed any new taxes on residents, but wants the state to assess a fee on corporations whose employees make so little they qualify for public healthcare. Hilton, a British American who was once a close adviser to former British Prime Minister David Cameron, ran on a deregulatory agenda, promising to slash environmental rules and the gas tax and allow more home construction on exurban, undeveloped land. One of his signature campaign promises was to eliminate the income tax on residents’ first $150,000 in earnings and make the income tax flat above that — amounting to an expensive tax cut for the highest earners that he’s said he would pay for with spending cuts. It’s one of his many promises that would need legislative approval, and he has not said how he would get Democrats in the Capitol to support them.
